To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lower social status is associated with higher cortisol and morbidity in a relatively egalitarian forager-horticulture society.
political influence is associated with lower cortisol and lower morbidity among egalitarian foraging-farming societies.
lower status is more deleterious to health in societies where leaders have more coercive authority, and where there is more to contest in terms of material wealth and resources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the health consequences of social rank, which is a fundamental dimension of human sociality.
the effects of status on health, and how this may vary across societies.
how social inequality influences health and well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
political influence is associated with lower cortisol and better health among egalitarian Tsimane’.

political influence is associated with lower cortisol and morbidity among Tsi-mane’ forager-farm-ers, but that these associations are mediated by access to social support, and that income may also be a factor.

low status is more benign among egalitarian societies, but that the effects of social status on cortisol and health can still be observed in these societies, and that these effects can be mediated by social support.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
political influence is associated with better health among egalitarian societies.
political influence, and the social support that comes with it, buffers the effects of chronic psychosocial and physiological stress among egalitarian foragers-farmers.
political influence, and the social capital that accompanies it, is associated with lower stress and better health among the Tsimane’.
The main takeaway from our work is that
political influence is associated with better health, and that this relationship is partly mediated through cortisol, which in turn is associated with morbidity.
the health costs of low status may be mitigated when social hierarchies are relatively egalitarian.
political influence is associated with lower stress hormone levels and better health in a society where leaders lack coercing authority and there is little material wealth to contest.
